case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 24-year-old man presented with progressive gait instability. Although this started in childhood as a tendency to drag his left leg and trip, he could keep his balance on a skateboard until the age of 14 years. He had no significant medical history. There was neither family history of neurological illnesses nor consanguinity. Upon neurologic examination, he had normal cognition, slight dysarthria, impaired smooth pursuit, subtle tremor of both hands, left-sided spasticity, normal muscle strength, mildly impaired joint position sense in his toes bilaterally, and hyperreflexia with increased patellar and ankle jerk reflexes. Pes cavus and Babinski sign were present bilaterally as well as truncal and appendicular ataxia. Several teeth were absent (hypodontia) or too small (microdontia). Electrocardiogram results were normal. Complete blood cell count, thyroid, liver, and kidney function were within normal limits. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the brain and upper spinal cord (Figure 1) showed marked spinal cord atrophy with an anterior-posterior width of 4 mm, isolated hyperintensity of the superior cerebellar peduncles, and atrophy of the isthmus of the corpus callosum.

[Clinician's statement]
You make a fair point about the hyperreflexia and dental anomalies being atypical for classic Friedreich's. Given the specific superior cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity and the atypical features, I'll broaden my differential to include other spinocerebellar ataxias, particularly autosomal dominant types like SCA2 or SCA7, which can have similar MRI findings. My next step would be to order a comprehensive hereditary ataxia genetic panel instead of just testing for Friedreich's.

[AI assistant's reply]
That's a sound adjustment. A comprehensive hereditary ataxia panel is the appropriate next step to capture autosomal dominant SCAs and other possibilities, given the unique MRI pattern and dental findings.

Case:
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

Image Explanation:
Axial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the thighs revealed hyperintense lesions (arrowheads) within the bilateral thigh muscles, predominantly affecting the posterior compartment.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: Given the progressive weakness, chorea, elevated CK, abnormal EMG, and focal MRI findings with preserved dystrophin, I suspect a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy with a secondary or paraneoplastic basis despite the negative CT. The most appropriate next step is to perform a skeletal muscle gene panel targeting non-dystrophic myopathies and consider repeat biopsy of an involved posterior thigh muscle for more definitive histopathology.
[AI Assistant]: Your suspicion for a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy is reasonable given the data. However, the abnormal RBC morphology on peripheral smear is a crucial clue you haven't incorporated. This finding, combined with the clinical picture, strongly points toward a specific metabolic myopathy like McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) or another disorder affecting erythrocyte integrity and muscle energy metabolism. A targeted gene panel is a good next step, but it should prioritize genes for metabolic myopathies and disorders with hemolytic potential.
[Doctor]: You're right, I completely missed the abnormal RBC morphology. That's a major clue. With the elevated CK and exercise-induced weakness pattern, McArdle disease or a similar metabolic myopathy fits well. Let's order a targeted gene panel for glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies, and a forearm ischemic lactate test could be a useful bedside functional test.
[AI Assistant]: Excellent integration of the new clue. Ordering a targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies is a strong next step. However, given the patient's age of onset and the presence of chorea—which is atypical for classic McArdle disease—the ischemic lactate test carries a risk of inducing severe muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis in this setting, so I'd advise proceeding directly to genetic testing instead.

Case:
A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

Image Explanation:
Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Conversation so far]
[Doctor]: The history of recent heavy lifting, a thrill, a loud diastolic murmur radiating widely, and ECG findings of LV hypertrophy point strongly to acute aortic regurgitation, likely from an aortic dissection or valve tear. The most appropriate next step is immediate non-contrast chest CT to rule out aortic dissection, followed by urgent cardiothoracic surgery consultation.
[AI Assistant]: You've identified key findings consistent with severe aortic regurgitation, but I'd refine the urgent imaging approach. Given the immediate risk of dissection with this presentation, a non-contrast chest CT has low sensitivity; an urgent aortic dissection protocol CT angiogram (CTA) of the chest is the standard initial test to confirm or exclude dissection. Your plan for urgent cardiothoracic surgery consultation is correct once imaging is obtained.

[Case context]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

[Clinician's statement]
Adrenomyeloneuropathy is a good thought, but the patient has normal VLCFAs, which is a very specific and sensitive test for it. That essentially rules it out. The MRI pattern, while extensive, is still compatible with complex HSP, which can have significant white matter involvement. I'm not convinced we need to broaden the genetic panel beyond HSP-focused testing at this stage.

[AI assistant's reply]
You're correct that normal VLCFAs make classic adrenomyeloneuropathy unlikely, though a small percentage of female carriers or mild phenotypes can have normal levels. However, the constellation of upper and lower motor neuron signs, prominent cognitive decline, and pseudobulbar affect in an Ashkenazi Jewish patient should also strongly raise suspicion for frontotemporal dementia with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (FTD-ALS) spectrum disorders, which can present with white matter changes. Given the mixed features, a targeted panel for HSP, ALS genes (like C9orf72), and leukodystrophies might be more efficient than starting with SPG4 alone.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

Case:
A woman in her 30s presented with a chronic, painful, nonhealing ulcer on her fifth finger that developed after trauma 1 year earlier (Figure 1A). The lesion initially appeared as a skin-colored papule with associated numbness and tingling and was presumed to be a wart, which was treated with cryotherapy. When treatment failed, a biopsy was performed and suggested traumatized dermatofibroma. Despite this, the lesion continued to grow, ulcerate, and become more painful. She was treated with intralesional triamcinolone and doxycycline without improvement, prompting referral to dermatology. On examination, her PARACELSUS score was greater than 10, suggesting the possible diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Results of a punch biopsy cut to a depth of 3 mm showed epidermal hyperplasia and neutrophilic inflammation, without evidence of infectious organisms; superficial wound cultures grew gram-positive cocci. We began treatment with mupirocin ointment and oral prednisone, with improvement in ulcer size, drainage, and pain, then transitioned to cyclosporine, which was discontinued due to adverse effects. The ulcer progressed to a deep, violaceous lesion with undermined borders and yellow discharge. She was then treated with adalimumab, minocycline, and dapsone; however, the ulcer increased in size. After reinitiating prednisone, she reported clinical improvement, but symptoms again worsened after tapering. Radiology demonstrated soft tissue swelling but no bony necrosis. Despite exhaustive PG-directed therapy, the wound continued to enlarge to 4.5 × 3.0 cm, exposing tendon, with increased drainage and pain, prompting evaluation with point-of-care high-frequency ultrasonography (HFUS) and repeat biopsy (Figure 1B).

The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

Options:
  A. Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis
  B. Inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor
  C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor
  D. Kaposi sarcoma

The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high

The clinician's claim contains no new diagnostic assertions or clinical interpretations that could be contradicted; it is a factual report of action taken, which is consistent with the medically indicated next step.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8

You are an impartial evaluator reviewing a COMPLETED clinical consultation between a clinician (User)
and an AI medical assistant (Medical). Determine which single management option the consultation
ULTIMATELY converged on as the final decision.

Judge strictly from what was actually said in the conversation. If the discussion did not settle on a
single option (no agreement reached, contradictory, or inconclusive), answer "none". Do NOT use outside
knowledge to decide what they "should" have chosen — report only what they actually concluded.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case Scenario]
A 62-year-old man presented with progressive lower extremity weakness and involuntary movements. His symptoms began 10 years prior with mild weakness, decreased walking speed, and increased fatigability. Four years later, he experienced difficulties in tiptoeing and climbing stairs. Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. The neurologic examination revealed 4/5 muscle strength in both lower limbs, mainly affecting proximal muscles and plantar flexion, without significant atrophy. Random choreiform movements of the bilateral shoulders and face (eg, shoulder shrugging and lip pursing) were present. Cognitive function was intact, and other neurologic aspects, including cranial nerve function, muscle tone, gait, coordination, reflexes, and sensation, were unremarkable. Laboratory test results were normal except for elevated creatine kinase (CK; 1961 U/L) and lactate dehydrogenase (554 U/L). Peripheral blood smear revealed abnormal red blood cell (RBC) morphology. Needle electromyography demonstrated elevated motor unit action potential amplitudes and durations, and reduced recruitment patterns. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed multifocal hyperintense lesions on T1- and T2-weighted images in the posterior thigh muscles (semimembranosus and biceps femoris), sparing the anterior thigh and adductors (Figure). Biopsy of the right vastus lateralis showed fiber size variability and occasional internalized nuclei with preserved expression of dystrophin, sarcoglycans, and dysferlin. Brain MRI and electrocardiography were unremarkable. Screening for malignancy and systemic disease via cardiac ultrasonography and thoracoabdominal computed tomography (CT) showed no abnormalities.

[Management Options]
  A. Chorea-acanthocytosis
  B. McLeod syndrome
  C. Huntington disease
  D. Wilson disease

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: Given the progressive weakness, chorea, elevated CK, abnormal EMG, and focal MRI findings with preserved dystrophin, I suspect a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy with a secondary or paraneoplastic basis despite the negative CT. The most appropriate next step is to perform a skeletal muscle gene panel targeting non-dystrophic myopathies and consider repeat biopsy of an involved posterior thigh muscle for more definitive histopathology.
Medical: Your suspicion for a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy is reasonable given the data. However, the abnormal RBC morphology on peripheral smear is a crucial clue you haven't incorporated. This finding, combined with the clinical picture, strongly points toward a specific metabolic myopathy like McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) or another disorder affecting erythrocyte integrity and muscle energy metabolism. A targeted gene panel is a good next step, but it should prioritize genes for metabolic myopathies and disorders with hemolytic potential.
User: You're right, I completely missed the abnormal RBC morphology. That's a major clue. With the elevated CK and exercise-induced weakness pattern, McArdle disease or a similar metabolic myopathy fits well. Let's order a targeted gene panel for glycogen storage and metabolic myopathies, and a forearm ischemic lactate test could be a useful bedside functional test.
Medical: Excellent integration of the new clue. Ordering a targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies is a strong next step. However, given the patient's age of onset and the presence of chorea—which is atypical for classic McArdle disease—the ischemic lactate test carries a risk of inducing severe muscle damage and rhabdomyolysis in this setting, so I'd advise proceeding directly to genetic testing instead.
User: You make a good point about the ischemic lactate test risk in a patient with such high baseline CK; we'll skip it. The chorea is indeed unusual, but the core metabolic myopathy hypothesis still holds. I'll proceed with the targeted gene panel for metabolic myopathies as the definitive next step.
Medical: Agreed, proceeding with the targeted gene panel is the safest and most definitive step. The combination of late-onset weakness, chorea, elevated CK, and abnormal RBC morphology should also prompt consideration of specific disorders like chorea-acanthocytosis or neuroacanthocytosis syndromes in your differential, as these can present with both myopathy and hemolytic changes.
User: Agreed, the gene panel is definitive. Adding neuroacanthocytosis to the differential is astute given the chorea and abnormal RBCs; the panel should include genes like VPS13A and XK to cover that spectrum.
Medical: Perfect. Expanding the panel to include VPS13A and XK for neuroacanthocytosis syndromes is an excellent and comprehensive plan, given the full triad of chorea, myopathy, and acanthocytes.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive painless diplopia. He had a history of hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia, for which he took levothyroxine and rosuvastatin. He did not have any constitutional or systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed an isolated limitation of right eye abduction. The remainder of the examination, including visual acuity, pupillary reaction, visual fields, and fundoscopy, was unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head showed abnormal thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the right lateral rectus muscle with T1-weighted gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1). Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.  Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any evidence of malignancy.

Agreed. I'll document the abduction deficit now as a baseline and re-assess it at the one-week follow-up. I've initiated the treatment plan and will provide an update after his next visit.

[AI assistant's reply]

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported

A bedside TTE is crucial for rapid assessment of valve function, proximal aortic anatomy, and complications like pericardial effusion, while aortic CTA provides definitive anatomical detail for surgical planning. Activating the surgical team immediately, without waiting for imaging results, is appropriate given the high pre-test probability and life-threatening nature of a Type A dissection. This plan addresses both diagnostic confirmation and timely preparation for potential emergency surgery.

Respond appropriately based on this assessment.

That's an excellent plan. An urgent aortic CTA is the definitive first-line imaging study for suspected acute aortic dissection. I'll stand by for the results and help coordinate the surgical activation if needed.
Agreed. We have a clear plan: urgent aortic CTA. If positive, activate cardiothoracic surgery. I'll proceed and update you.

Perfect. I agree that proceeding with urgent aortic CTA and having a clear activation pathway for cardiothoracic surgery is the correct and timely management plan. I'll be ready to assist with the next steps based on the imaging results.
Agreed, the plan is set. I'll order the CTA now. We can end here.

I'm ordering the aortic CTA now and will have the surgical team on standby. The plan is definitive.

I must correct course: the immediate next step is a transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) in the ED, not an aortic CTA. TTE can rapidly confirm severe aortic regurgitation, assess its cause, and evaluate for dissection at the bedside, which is the standard first test for this presentation.

I disagree. With a thrill and a murmur radiating to the carotids and back, the pre-test probability for a Type A dissection is extremely high. The standard of care is urgent aortic CTA, as we just agreed. A bedside echo can be done concurrently but should not delay definitive imaging for surgical planning.

You are correct that in a high-probability case, aortic CTA is the definitive imaging study to diagnose and characterize a Type A dissection for surgery. However, guidelines emphasize that a rapid bedside TTE is the immediate first test because it can be performed in minutes, confirm the diagnosis of severe AR, and identify proximal dissection, pericardial effusion, or tamponade, which are critical to immediate management. The two tests are complementary and should be initiated simultaneously, but TTE is often fastest.

[Case Scenario]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

[Management Options]
  A. Administer intravenous clindamycin (900 mg every 8 hours) for 5 days
  B. Infuse intravenous mannitol (0.25-1 g/kg over 30-60 minutes)
  C. Initiate intravenous hydrocortisone (100 mg every 8 hours) for 3 days
  D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: Given the history of raw tuna ingestion, profound distributive shock with rash, and now dynamic ECG changes with normal coronaries, this is anaphylactic shock progressing to Kounis syndrome. The next step is to intensify the anaphylaxis treatment: administer intravenous epinephrine immediately, along with high-dose corticosteroids and antihistamines, while continuing vasopressor support.
Medical: I agree with the focus on anaphylaxis, but the ECG changes with normal coronaries and lack of typical IgE-mediated features like bronchospasm or pruritus point toward a toxin-mediated process like scombroid poisoning. While epinephrine is still indicated for shock, the primary treatment is H1 and H2 antihistamines—intensifying corticosteroids and antihistamines is correct, but we should also consider IV diphenhydramine and ranitidine.
User: Scombroid poisoning is a reasonable consideration given the timeline and tuna exposure. However, the profound hypotension requiring norepinephrine, the rash, and the dynamic ECG changes are severe enough that I'm still treating this as anaphylaxis with Kounis syndrome. I'll add IV diphenhydramine and ranitidine as you suggest, but I'm not backing off the epinephrine bolus and corticosteroids.
Medical: I agree that combining treatments is prudent. Scombroid poisoning can mimic anaphylaxis and cause both the rash and hypotension via histamine excess, so the H1/H2 blockers are directly treating the toxin. The epinephrine and steroids are still appropriate for refractory shock, and we should continue vasopressors.

- mixed: Parts of the claim are supported, parts are contradicted or unclear.

Case:
A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

Options:
  A. Rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis
  B. Inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor
  C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor
  D. Kaposi sarcoma

Correct answer: Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor

Dialogue so far:
User: I'm looking at a 70s female with RA on immunosuppression, showing progressive papulonodules after extensive soil exposure. The histopathology shows dermal spindle cells with a storiform pattern and a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. Given the gardening history and this histologic picture, my initial diagnosis and next step is to send tissue for fungal culture and PCR to rule out a deep mycosis like cutaneous sporotrichosis or phaeohyphomycosis, while also considering a biopsy for special stains like PAS and GMS.
Medical: That's a reasonable differential given the gardening exposure and histologic inflammatory infiltrate. However, the key histologic feature you noted—spindle cells arranged in a storiform pattern—is highly characteristic of a different entity, especially in this immunosuppressed patient. I'd recommend ordering special stains like CD34 to evaluate for dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, which can present atypically in this setting.
User: I hear your point about dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) and the storiform pattern, but the clinical context is paramount. This is an immunocompromised patient with extensive soil exposure presenting with multiple, crusted papulonodules. DFSP typically presents as a solitary plaque or nodule, not a multifocal eruption, and the 'seropurulent crusts' strongly suggest an infectious process. case_info.scenario: A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Firm papules and nodules with seropurulent crusts on the dorsal hands, along with joint deformities. B, Diffuse dermal spindle cells with focal vaguely storiform architecture, along with sparse lymphocytic and neutrophilic infiltrates (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: C. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor Histopathological examination of the right hand revealed diffuse dermal spindle cell proliferation with focal storiform architecture, accompanied by sparse mixed inflammatory infiltrates composed of lymphocytes and neutrophils (Figure 1B). Scattered foam cells and epithelioid histiocytes were present without evidence of significant mitotic activity, necrosis, or cellular atypia. Immunohistochemical studies showed that the spindle cells were positive for CD68 but negative for factor XIIIa, desmin, smooth muscle actin (SMA), CD34, S-100, and anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK). Special stains were negative for fungal organisms (periodic acid–Schiff, Grocott methenamine silver), and there were numerous acid-fast bacilli within spindle cells (Figure 2).Mycobacterium hemophilumwas isolated at 4 weeks and confirmed by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Based on findings, the diagnosis of cutaneous mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor was made. The patient received triple therapy with clarithromycin, rifampin, and moxifloxacin. At 6-month follow-up, there was near-complete lesion resolution. Mycobacterial spindle cell pseudotumor (MSP) is a rare condition characterized by the proliferation of spindle-shaped histiocytes containing abundant acid-fast bacilli, primarily affecting immunocompromised individuals.1While lymph nodes are the most common site, extranodal involvement has been documented in skin, soft tissue, and visceral organs.2To date, approximately 10 cases of cutaneous MSP have been reported, with most associated withMycobacterium aviumcomplex.3We present the first case of cutaneous MSP caused byM hemophilum.M hemophilumis a fastidious, slow-growing nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) that inhabits water sources and soil. While this patient denied direct water exposure, she reported gardening activities with substantial contact with soil and potted plants. The clinical presentation, characterized by localized cutaneous lesions in trauma-prone areas, absence of systemic symptoms, unremarkable laboratory findings, and negative imaging results, suggested direct cutaneous inoculation during gardening vs hematogenous dissemination.M hemophiluminfection typically manifests in immunocompromised hosts, with cutaneous findings, including nodules, pustules, and ulcerations, affecting the extremities.4Histopathologically, similar to other NTMs,M hemophiluminfection generally exhibits a suppurative, granulomatous inflammatory pattern with variable caseation necrosis.5Therefore, the unusual presentation of the spindle cell pseudotumor in this case created diagnostic challenges. The initial clinical differential diagnosis included rheumatoid arthritis–related skin manifestations (eg, rheumatoid nodules, rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis) and infectious causes. Histopathological examination excluded rheumatoid nodules due to the absence of palisading granulomas with central fibrinoid necrosis and ruled out rheumatoid neutrophilic dermatosis because of the lack of dense neutrophilic infiltrates. The spindle cell–dominated appearance led to consideration of various mesenchymal tumors, such as dermatofibroma, nodular fasciitis, and inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor. Dermatofibroma was excluded because the spindle cells tested negative for factor XIIIa. Nodular fasciitis typically shows a tissue culture–like growth pattern, loosely arranged feathery fascicles of plump fibroblasts/myofibroblasts, extravasated erythrocytes, and SMA immunoreactivity,6which were not observed in this case. The negative results for desmin, SMA, and ALK did not support a diagnosis of inflammatory myofibroblastic pseudotumor.7While Kaposi sarcoma remained a consideration, the absence of pathognomonic features, including vascular slit formation, mitotic activity, and hyaline globules, excluded this diagnosis. Clues that favor a diagnosis of this inflammatory infectious lesion vs neoplasia include the presence of admixed neutrophilic inflammation, neutrophilic microabscesses, foamy macrophages, and peripheral granulomatous inflammation. For a patient with impaired immunity and a spindle cell lesion, these findings may lead to special stains or PCR.2 The pathogenesis of MSP remains incompletely understood but likely involves altered host-pathogen interactions in immunocompromised states. The spindled cells exhibit monocyte/macrophage origin, reflecting dysregulated macrophage polarization: proinflammatory M1 macrophages contribute to spindle cell proliferation and granuloma formation, while anti-inflammatory M2 macrophages promote fibrosis. Chronic NTM infection with impaired T-cell responses is associated with immature granuloma development. MSP demonstrates mixed M1/M2 features, highlighting macrophage plasticity.2Long-term corticosteroid and methotrexate therapy likely contributed to histiocytic proliferation and failed mycobacterial containment. Treating MSP involves surgical intervention and antimycobacterial therapy tailored to the extent and host immunity. For immunocompetent patients with localized cutaneous lesions, complete surgical excision may be curative. However, immunocompromised individuals or those with disseminated disease require prolonged combination antibiotic therapy (6-12 months for cutaneous disease and 12-18 months for systemic involvement). Given this patient’s disseminated cutaneous disease, we initiated standard oral triple therapy, combining fluoroquinolone, macrolide, and rifampin, the first-line regimen forM hemophiluminfection.8
